title: Saving
description: Emergency funds, savings goals, and how compound interest makes money grow by itself.

lessons.title: Why save at all?
body: Saving is just spending later, on purpose. It lets you buy big things (a car, a laptop, a trip) without borrowing.
Saving also buys you choices. With money set aside you can say no to a bad job, handle a surprise bill, or jump on a good deal.
Start small. Saving $10 a week is $520 a year. The habit matters more than the amount.
lessons.example: Your car needs a $400 repair. With savings, it's a bad day. Without savings, it's a credit card balance with interest.

lessons.title: The emergency fund
body: An emergency fund is money saved only for real surprises: a car repair, a medical bill, losing your job.

Step 1: Save a starter fund of $500 to $1,000.
Step 2: Later, grow it to 3 to 6 months of your needs.
A new phone because you want one is not an emergency. A cracked phone you need for work might be.
lessons.keyIdea: Keep your emergency fund separate so you don't spend it by accident.
lessons.example: Your needs cost $1,200 a month. A 3-month fund = 3 × $1,200 = $3,600.

lessons.title: Setting a savings goal
body: Good goals are specific: what, how much, and by when.
To find how long it takes: (Goal − Already saved) ÷ Saved per week. Round up, because you can't finish in part of a week.
Too slow? You can save more each week, pick a cheaper goal, or give yourself more time.
lessons.keyIdea: Weeks to goal = (goal − saved) ÷ per week, rounded up.
lessons.example: Goal: $300 headphones. Saved: $40. Saving $20 a week → (300 − 40) ÷ 20 = 13 weeks.

lessons.title: Compound interest: money that grows itself
body: Interest is money a bank pays you for keeping your money there.
Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Each month, the interest gets added to your balance, so next month you earn interest on a bigger amount.
The secret ingredient is time. Starting at 16 instead of 26 can mean a lot more money later, even with the same deposits.
lessons.keyIdea: The earlier you start, the more work compound interest does for you.
lessons.example: $100 a month at 5% a year: after 30 years about $83,000. After 40 years about $153,000. The last 10 years add about $69,000.

lessons.title: Where to keep your savings
body: A savings account keeps money separate from your spending money. A high-yield savings account pays more interest than a regular one.
Look for accounts insured by the FDIC (banks) or NCUA (credit unions). Insured means your money is protected up to $250,000 even if the bank fails.
A jar at home earns no interest and can be lost or stolen. Investing (like stocks) can grow more over many years but can also go down, so it's for long-term money, not emergencies.
lessons.keyIdea: Emergency money: safe and easy to reach. Long-term money: can grow in investments.
lessons.example: Your car fund for next year goes in a high-yield savings account, not the stock market.

practice.prompt: Your goal is $300. You have $40 saved and can save $20 a week. How many weeks until you reach it?
Goal: $250 concert trip. Saved: $0. You save $15 a week. How many weeks? (Round up.)
practice.explanation: $250 ÷ $15 = 16.67. You can't stop partway through a week, so round up to 17 weeks.

practice.prompt: Your needs cost $1,500 a month. How big is a 3-month emergency fund?
You put $200 in an account that pays 5% interest once a year. How much is in the account after 2 years? (Interest compounds yearly.)
practice.explanation: Year 1: $200 × 1.05 = $210. Year 2: $210 × 1.05 = $220.50. Year 2 earned more because it earned interest on the first year's interest.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a real emergency for your emergency fund?
choices: Your car breaks down and you need it to get to work
practice.explanation: An emergency is surprising and necessary. A sale or a new game is neither.

practice.prompt: You start with $1,000, add $50 at the end of every month, and earn 6% a year compounded monthly. About how much do you have after 10 years?
practice.explanation: You put in $1,000 + $50 × 120 = $7,000. Interest adds about $3,013 more, for about $10,013. Try it in the Compound Interest tool!

quiz.prompt: What's a good first target for a starter emergency fund?
choices: You don't need one if you have a credit card
quiz.explanation: A starter fund of $500 to $1,000 covers most small surprises. Grow it to 3 to 6 months of needs later.

quiz.prompt: Goal: $600 laptop. Saved: $150. Saving $25 a week. How many weeks to go?
What makes compound interest different from simple interest?
choices: You earn interest on your past interest too
quiz.explanation: Compounding adds interest to your balance, so later interest is earned on a bigger amount.

quiz.prompt: Two people each save $100 a month at 5%. One starts 10 years earlier. What does the early starter get from those extra 10 years?
quiz.explanation: After 40 years: about $152,600. After 30 years: about $83,200. Difference: about $69,000, even though the extra deposits were only $12,000. That's time doing the work.

choices: Makes your account earn more interest
Protects your bank deposits (up to $250,000) if the bank fails
quiz.explanation: FDIC (banks) and NCUA (credit unions) insure deposits up to $250,000 per person, per bank, per account type.

quiz.prompt: You save $10 a week for a whole year (52 weeks). How much have you saved, not counting interest?
Where's the best place for your emergency fund?
choices: In stocks, so it grows fast
In a savings account that's separate from your spending account
In a jar in your closet
quiz.explanation: Emergency money should be safe and easy to reach, but not so easy that you spend it by accident.

flashcards.back: Money saved only for real surprises. Start with $500–$1,000, grow to 3–6 months of needs.
Earning interest on your interest, so growth speeds up over time.
(Goal − saved) ÷ amount per week, rounded up.
A savings account that pays a higher interest rate than a regular one.
Government insurance that protects bank / credit union deposits up to $250,000.
How much a bank pays you per year, as a percent of your balance.
